summary: Taiwan doesn't name the roof rat as either permitted or banned for pet-keeping, so its status is mixed and partly unsettled — but importing one is the hard wall. Pet rats (mainly fancy rats, R. norvegicus) are sold openly and covered by the Animal Protection Act's broad 'pet' definition, and the May-2026 641-species ownership-ban list doesn't appear to name R. rattus. The open question is whether R. rattus is on the Wildlife Conservation Act's captive-bred-wild-animal registration list (Art. 55) — if so, keeping/breeding a captive individual needs Forestry Agency registration. Selling/giving falls in a gap: the 'specified pet' business-licence regime covers only dogs and cats, so rodent sales are neither licensed nor clearly sanctioned. IMPORT is effectively very difficult: live rodents need a trade import permit + a WCA wildlife-import permit + APHIA quarantine (cargo only, ≥7-day isolation, origin health certificate), and given R. rattus's invasive-pest status plus active urban rat-control campaigns, approval is unlikely in practice.

kit.problem: In Taiwan, pet rats are sold and kept openly, and the Animal Protection Act's broad definition of "pet" doesn't exclude the roof rat (Rattus rattus, 屋頂鼠/玄鼠). But the rules never actually name R. rattus, so a keeper is left guessing on two points. First, it is unclear whether R. rattus is on the Wildlife Conservation Act's "captive-bred terrestrial wild animal" list (Art. 55) — if it is, keeping or breeding even a captive-born individual would need Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency registration; if it isn't, no such registration applies. Second, the "Specified Pet Business" licensing regime that governs breeding and welfare standards covers ONLY dogs and cats, so pet rats fall into a gap with no clear welfare protection and no licensing pathway. Layered on top is the species' reputation: R. rattus is an invasive urban pest, and 2026 rat-control campaigns mean officials may not distinguish a tame, captive-bred companion animal from a wild city rat. Importing one is effectively a wall (trade permit + wildlife-import permit + cargo-only quarantine, approval unlikely), but the everyday question for someone already keeping a captive-bred pet is simply: what's my legal status, and is the welfare gap going to be fixed?
kit.ask: Ask the Ministry of Agriculture for a plain written answer to two questions: (1) Is captive-bred Rattus rattus on the Wildlife Conservation Act Art. 55 captive-bred-wildlife list — and on the May-2026 ownership-ban list under Animal Protection Act Art. 8 — and if so, what does a private hobbyist need to register to keep and breed captive-born individuals? (2) Will the Ministry extend "specified pet" welfare and breeding rules (currently dogs and cats only) to cover pet rats, so captive-bred companion rats get the same baseline protection? Separately, supporters can back the existing 台灣愛鼠協會 (Rodentscare) campaign and write to a Legislative Yuan member asking that pet rats be recognized as specified pets. Throughout, make the distinction clear: this is about a tame, captive-bred, indoor companion animal that is never released — not about wild urban rats or pest control.
kit.branch_note: HYBRID, leaning AGENCY/CLARIFICATION. Two distinct problems with two distinct levers. (A) The keeping/breeding status of captive-bred R. rattus is genuinely UNSETTLED, not banned — the law (APA Art. 3) covers it as a "pet," but nobody has confirmed whether it sits on the WCA Art. 55 captive-wildlife registration list or the 2026 ownership-ban annex. That ambiguity is a BUREAUCRATIC reading problem: the right lever is the AGENCY (Ministry of Agriculture), via a written clarification / declaratory answer through its official Chief's Mailbox. You are not asking it to change a law, only to state plainly how existing law applies to a captive-bred companion animal — which it can do. (B) The welfare/licensing GAP (specified-pet rules name only dogs and cats) is a LAW/RULEMAKING problem: that is written into the Specified Pet Business Management Regulations, and no amount of asking the agency to "interpret" it will add rats — it has to be amended. So for that piece, say it plainly: the fix is rulemaking/legislation, pursued through the active 台灣愛鼠協會 campaign and a message to a Legislative Yuan member, not an appeal to the enforcement desk. Net: lead with the agency clarification (cheap, fast, resolves the live uncertainty), and route the protection-gap ask to the legislative/advocacy channel where it actually belongs.

This is the right place to ask for a WRITTEN clarification: whether captive-bred R. rattus is on the WCA Art. 55 list or the 2026 ownership-ban annex, and whether 'specified pet' rules will be extended to rats. template.en:
To the Ministry of Agriculture,

I am writing about the legal status and welfare of pet rats kept in Taiwan. Pet rats are sold and kept openly here, and the Animal Protection Act defines a "pet" broadly, but the rules never specifically name the roof rat (Rattus rattus, 屋頂鼠/玄鼠), which leaves keepers genuinely unsure of their position.

I would be grateful for a written answer: (1) Is captive-bred Rattus rattus on the Wildlife Conservation Act Article 55 captive-bred-wildlife list, or on the May 2026 ownership-restriction list under Animal Protection Act Article 8? If so, what registration does a private hobbyist need to keep and breed captive-born individuals? (2) Will the Ministry extend the "specified pet" welfare and breeding standards — currently limited to dogs and cats — to cover pet rats?

Please note this concerns tame, captive-bred companion animals kept entirely indoors. They are never released into the wild and are not connected to wild urban rats or pest control.

Thank you for your guidance.

[Your name]
[Your city / contact]

敬致農業部：

本人就在台灣飼養之寵物鼠的法律地位與福利問題提出詢問。寵物鼠在台灣公開販售與飼養，《動物保護法》對「寵物」的定義亦相當廣泛，然而相關法規從未明確列名屋頂鼠（玄鼠，學名 Rattus rattus），致使飼主對自身的合法地位實感不確定。

懇請惠予書面說明：(一) 人工繁殖之屋頂鼠（Rattus rattus）是否列於《野生動物保育法》第55條之人工飼養繁殖野生動物名單，或列於2026年5月依《動物保護法》第8條公告之禁止飼養物種名單？若是，私人飼主欲飼養及繁殖人工繁殖之個體，須辦理何種登記？(二) 農業部是否將把目前僅限於犬、貓之「特定寵物」福利與繁殖管理規範，擴及至寵物鼠？

謹此說明：本案所指為性情溫馴、人工繁殖、完全於室內飼養之伴侶動物。牠們絕不會被野放，與野生都市鼠類或鼠害防治並無關聯。

感謝貴部惠予指引。

keep.why: The Animal Protection Act (APA) Art. 3 defines 'pet' broadly and doesn't exclude R. rattus; pet rats are sold/kept in Taiwan. BUT if R. rattus is on the Wildlife Conservation Act (WCA) Art. 55 captive-bred-wild-animal list, keeping a captive individual needs Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency registration — its inclusion couldn't be confirmed. The May-2026 641-species ownership ban (APA Art. 8) doesn't appear to name R. rattus (full annex unverified). Genuinely unsettled → confirm with the authorities.
keep.governing_law: Animal Protection Act Art. 3, Art. 8; Wildlife Conservation Act Art. 55.

breed.why: The Specified Pet Business Regulations cover only dogs and cats, so rodents sit outside that licensing framework — a hobbyist breeding R. rattus faces no explicit prohibition IF the species isn't on the WCA Art. 55 captive-bred-wildlife list (which would require Forestry Agency approval to breed). No published ruling authorizes or prohibits it; invasive-pest status may draw extra scrutiny.
breed.governing_law: Specified Pet Business Mgmt Regulations (dogs/cats only); WCA Art. 55.

sell_give.why: Selling/giving R. rattus domestically isn't covered by the specified-pet licence regime (dogs/cats only); pet stores sell rats/hamsters without such a permit, so non-dog/cat rodent sales operate in a regulatory gap — neither licensed nor expressly forbidden. If WCA Art. 55 registration applies, display/sale of registered animals needs separate approval (WCA Art. 24). For-profit commercial breeding of an invasive species could attract public-health/environmental scrutiny.
sell_give.governing_law: Specified Pet Business Mgmt Regulations; WCA Art. 24.

transport.why: IMPORT is effectively very difficult: live rodents need (1) a trade import permit (restricted item given invasive/quarantine-pest status), (2) a WCA Art. 24 wildlife-import permit, and (3) APHIA quarantine — cargo shipment only (travellers may NOT hand-carry live rodents), ≥7-day post-arrival isolation, official origin health certificate filed 30+ days ahead. No published pathway for a hobbyist to import R. rattus, and approval is unlikely given its top-100 invasive status + 2026 rat-control campaigns. INTERNAL transport of a lawfully-kept animal isn't separately restricted (unless WCA-registered). Never release.
transport.governing_law: Animal & Animal Product Import Quarantine Conditions; APHIA quarantine procedures; WCA Art. 24.

restrictions.summary: Importing a live roof rat into Taiwan is effectively very hard: it needs a trade import permit + a wildlife-import permit + APHIA quarantine (cargo only, ≥7-day isolation, origin health certificate), and approval is unlikely given invasive-pest status. Hand-carrying live rodents is not allowed. Confirm keeping/breeding status (WCA Art. 55 list) with the Ministry of Agriculture before acquiring. Never release.
